item.title: In Gaza, we’ve seen horror unfold with global powers’ support. Is that a blueprint for horror elsewhere? | Ahdaf Soueif
item.description:
For now, it is Palestinians who are being killed and displaced. But ideologies of supremacy and domination threaten us all

Last week, Itamar Ben-Gvir, Israel’s minister of national security, put out an AI-generated video that showed a conveyor belt of overweight Palestinian prisoners – dreaming of food and education – entering one of his prisons; he pops the dream bubbles above their heads and they come out emaciated and crying. Ben-Gvir is building an execution site for Palestinian prisoners with spectator booths, and he recently showed up at Damon prison in northern Israel and taunted female prisoners who complained about the poor conditions. He is digging a moat around a new high-security jail and planning to introduce crocodiles to patrol it. In all this, he has the approval of Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, while the law that he championed mandating the death penalty for Palestinians deemed terrorists by military courts and convicted for lethal attacks is built on public support.

Sometime around 2017, many Palestinians and their supporters in the global media felt a change. Articles about Palestine no longer drew the hate mail we’d been accustomed to and events in support of Palestinian rights were hardly heckled. It seemed that people were less and less convinced by the image long cultivated by Israel and its supporters – the bearer of “western values” in the Middle East, the home to the “most moral army in the world”, a country acting only in self-defence – while it regularly assaulted Gaza and continued to expand its illegal settlements in the West Bank.

Can 'America First' survive Trump's war-first presidency?
item.description:
In a Thursday address at the GOP midterm convention that exalted President Donald Trump and demeaned his opponents as “extremists who openly hate our nation,” Vice President JD Vance hardly spoke about foreign policy.

He did not mention the war in Iran directly, and he only brought up foreign policy as an example of an issue that divides the party’s base. He urged voters not to “throw the baby out with the bathwater” because “you happen to disagree with us on a policy issue here or there.”

The acknowledgement of foreign policy as a divisive issue in the MAGA coalition is a stark retreat for Vance, who staked his 2023 endorsement of Trump on the fact that “he started no wars despite enormous pressure from his own party and even members of his own administration,” framing the president’s America First record as a much-needed deviation from decades of bipartisan hawkishness.

A few wars later, Vance appears to have backed down from the anti-war aspects of the America First movement. Meanwhile, in response to the Iran war and the administration’s supposed betrayal of its campaign promises, the Institute for Peace & Diplomacy has launched “Reclaiming America First,” an initiative meant to take back that mantle from what it describes as Trump's hawkish drift, and to articulate an alternative vision for American foreign policy.

Arta Moeini, director of research at the Institute for Peace & Diplomacy and one of the project leads, laid out the parameters he believes should guide an “America First” approach during a Thursday panel marking the launch of the event: it should be neither ideological nor partisan, nor tied to any one individual; it should be grounded in realism; and it should prioritize core U.S. security interests and domestic renewal while rejecting unilateralism and nativism.

“Trump has shown himself to be at least disingenuous about using the term ‘America First,’” Moeini said during the panel, adding that part of the inspiration for the discussion was to combat “the taint of that association of ‘America First’ with this version of Trump.”

That question of who actually carries the tradition forward inevitably turned to Vance, long seen as its standard-bearer within the administration, but whose own words offer a measure of how far the movement’s foreign policy rhetoric has shifted since Trump’s return to office.

While panelists mostly agreed that an “America First” foreign policy was likely only to come from a conservative U.S. president, the group's read on Vance as the steward of that vision was more measured. Moeini said Vance would have been “smart enough not to go to war" with Iran, even if he might not be the right person to fix U.S. foreign policy in the Middle East.

Michael Brendan Dougherty, a senior writer for the National Review, offered a grimly ironic assessment of how a more realist foreign policy could take hold in a hypothetical Vance administration.

“If Vance is elected president after Donald Trump, he’s going to be looking at a munitions stockpile that is very depleted, and will be discouraging of him taking on unpredictable gambles. That’s not the way you want restraint to [be achieved], but it is the way it’s going now,” he said. “The Iran war is bringing about a humiliation of America, and that will bring along at least some restraint.”

Dougherty also pointed to the constraining effect of public opinion, saying that American opposition to war may have prevented Trump from taking even more dramatic steps in Iran, such as an invasion of Kharg Island.

There is evidence that elements of Trump’s base have turned against him as a result of this war. A recent survey from Navigator Research found that roughly 20% of Trump 2024 voters regret their decision. Among that group, almost half cited the war with Iran as the primary reason for their regret.

There were real policy disagreements over what "America First" meant. Daniel McCarthy, editor of Modern Age, warned that talk of a "multinodal" world echoes liberal internationalism and misreads an American public that is still proud of the country, while the panel also split over whether to encourage or deter a Polish or Japanese nuclear program. But all the panelists agreed that America First is a foreign policy movement that both predates and will outlive Trump.

“America First as an ordering principle of American statecraft will long outlive MAGA and the current coalitional dynamics at play surrounding the president,” Reid Smith, Vice President for Foreign Policy at Stand Together, said.

item.title: Call it the Miliband doctrine. Let’s hope the new Israeli settlement boycott is just the start | Steve Bloomfield
item.description:
This week’s move suggests that, even in the age of Trump, Britain will once again have an ‘ethical dimension’ to its foreign policy. That’s good for the world

Almost 30 years ago, the Labour titan Robin Cook announced his arrival at the Foreign Office by laying out what would become described as an “ethical foreign policy”. The UK, he said, “must support the demands of other peoples for the democratic rights on which we insist for ourselves”. Human rights would be “at the heart of our foreign policy”.

In the 25 years since Cook was demoted, Britain has had a further 14 foreign secretaries – including seven in the past six years – few of whom can claim to have placed progressive ideals at the heart of their actions. Ed Miliband’s speech on Tuesday outlining the UK’s decision to impose economic sanctions on Israeli settlements in the West Bank – and unveiling the international coalition he has built to support it – suggests that Cook may finally have a successor.

Steve Bloomfield is the former international editor of the Observer and a previous winner of the Orwell prize

item.title: Putin would rather keep killing than admit he’s lost. As a winter of misery looms in Ukraine, Nato must step in | Simon Tisdall
item.description:
The Russian leader is ploughing on with his forever war – and each day is a crime against humanity. Western democracies cannot simply sit on their hands

Ukraine’s people face a winter from hell. Thwarted on the battlefield, Russia is stepping up systematic, daily attacks on civilians, their homes, schools, hospitals, workplaces, and the vital infrastructure that sustains human life. Wave after wave of terrifying daytime ballistic missile and jet-drone strikes on Kyiv and other cities are destroying supermarket distribution hubs, pharmaceutical and medical facilities, logistics centres and warehouses. The result is sharply rising civilian casualties and growing shortages of food and other essentials. As a freezing winter approaches, Russia will again try to blow up Ukraine’s water supplies and power grid, cutting off electricity to millions. This is Vladimir Putin’s version of darkness at noon. He’d rather kill everybody than admit he’s lost.

Russia’s leader reportedly told Donald Trump this week that his “special military operation”, now in its fifth year, was going to plan. Trump may believe him. Western analysts certainly don’t. Failing militarily and taking huge casualties, his regime is under growing domestic economic and public pressure to wind down the war. Yet Putin seems to think one last big push can finally break Ukraine’s will. Trump’s renewed meddling – after months of inertia, he sent his patsy envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, back to Moscow last weekend (they also visited Kyiv for the first time) – perpetuates Kremlin delusions of victory. Now there’s talk of more talks. And all the while, Putin kills and kills. Each day is a crime against humanity.

Simon Tisdall is a Guardian foreign affairs commentator

Against the odds, BRICS overcomes sharp divisions in New Delhi
item.description:
The 18th summit of BRICS, a grouping with ten members including Brazil, China, India, Indonesia, Russia, and South Africa, concluded in New Delhi with a leaders declaration — a clear success for an event that brought together a deeply divided group of countries, including some currently fighting on either side of a war in the Middle East.

Key world leaders attended, including Chinese President Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, and Egyptian leader Abdel Fattah el-Sisi. There was, of course, the expected pageantry. Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim even belted out a 1960s Bollywood hit at the leaders’ dinner party to the admiration of his Indian hosts.

This success was not guaranteed. Just a few months previously, BRICS foreign ministers had failed to agree to a joint statement amid acrimonious exchanges between Iran and the United Arab Emirates, which have exchanged missile barrages amid the ongoing war in the Middle East. Despite these serious rifts, host India managed to pull off a declaration that everyone signed on to.

The price of this success, however, was much-watered down language on the Middle East war. The summit declaration in Rio de Janeiro last year had come out swinging, stating that “we condemn the military strikes against the Islamic Republic of Iran since 13 June 2025, which constitute a violation of international law and the Charter of the United Nations.” In New Delhi this past weekend, the grouping merely expressed “deep concern over the continued escalation of tensions in Middle East/West Asia.” It recalled “our respective national positions” and called for “exercising maximum restraint, as well as avoiding actions that could further aggravate the situation.”

Admittedly, India’s task was tougher than Brazil’s had been, with the war having escalated since late February 2026 to include the UAE as a combatant. It is extremely difficult for a club to reach any sort of consensus if two of its members are physically brawling. From this perspective, the New Delhi declaration was a win for India. But it was more a relief than a victory for BRICS as a whole. The grouping did not need the distraction at this critical juncture in its journey.

Beyond the Iran-U.S. war, there were other notable aspects to the declaration. Mysteriously, all references to the Ukraine conflict were dropped. The European war had been consistently mentioned in BRICS declarations since Russia invaded in 2022. Last year, the text had even included language that largely reflected the Russian position on Ukrainian attacks on three sites.

One welcome new feature of the text was a paragraph on Cuba, expressing "deep concern" on the "tightening of unilateral blockade measures (and) their adverse effects on the Cuban economy...and the worrying humanitarian impact on the Cuban people.” U.S. pressure on Cuba has grown manifold since last year. Havana is now a “partner country” within BRICS, a lower tier of membership. The text was clearly a nod to its concerns. But feelings against the embargo and blockade against Cuba run high in the United Nations. Practically all member states have repeatedly gone on record opposing them.

Like last year, Israel was mentioned by name and criticized for its actions in Lebanon. The text also maintained the strong language on Gaza from earlier years. Concern was expressed at "arrangements that may prejudice the inalienable rights of the Palestinian people and legitimize or prolong occupation." There were no references to the U.S.-initiated "Board of Peace" in the text, even though BRICS states Egypt, Indonesia, and UAE are among its members, as are partner countries Kazakhstan and Vietnam.

Finally, the text expressed strong criticism of the “imposition of unilateral coercive measures that are contrary to international law,” emphasizing that “unilateral economic sanctions and secondary sanctions, have far-reaching negative implications for the human rights, including the rights to development, health and food security, of the general population of targeted states.” It further characterized such measures as “undermin(ing) international law and the principles and purposes of the UN Charter.” This language was a clear dig at the United States and its European allies. Many Global South states feel highly vulnerable to the U.S.-led global sanctions regime.

Having launched some successful initiatives like the New Development Bank, and with its major expansion phase now behind it, BRICS finds itself at a crossroads. The growing pains of expansion are manifest, and the outbreak of multiple wars in the world couldn’t have come at a worse time. It will take some time for new members to be adequately socialized in the grouping. Over the next year or two, BRICS will need to take a deep breath and find its footing again if it is not to lose its mojo.

item.title: Push to sanction Serbia could empower leader it aims to hurt
item.description:
On August 27, Reps. Joe Wilson (R-S.C.) and Bill Keating (D-Mass.) introduced the SRBIJA Act, which would impose sanctions and visa restrictions on “malign actors” accused of undermining democracy, the rule of law, human rights, and stability in the Western Balkans. The proposed legislation also threatens sanctions on Serbia if Belgrade maintains its relationships with Russia, China, and Iran.

The initiative comes as Serbia prepares for snap parliamentary elections next month, following nearly two years of anti-government protests and shortly after Washington and Belgrade launched a new Strategic Dialogue. In Serbia’s polarized political environment, supporters of President Aleksandar Vučić portray Wilson and Keating as hostile foreign actors seeking to dictate Belgrade’s foreign policy, while opponents of the government largely see the SRBIJA Act positively and hope it will “ultimately lead to [Vučić’s] downfall,” said Nikola Mikovic, a Serbian geopolitical analyst.

The SRBIJA Act’s sponsors hope their legislative push will pressure Belgrade to abandon its delicate balancing act between the West, Moscow, and Beijing. But the bill could instead give Vučić an opportunity to strengthen the geopolitical narrative that he has shrewdly navigated a multipolar world, which resonates with many Serbian voters and has helped keep him at the helm.

Engaging Belgrade pragmatically


The SRBIJA Act does not represent the Trump administration’s approach to Serbia, underscored by the newly established Strategic Dialogue. Launched in July, it provides an institutional framework for continued bilateral engagement and cooperation across areas including energy and economics. The Trump administration will not abandon that framework because of a single bill in Congress.

Vladimir Trapara, a Belgrade-based political analyst, said the congressional initiative “stands poor chances of success” and argued that its failure could, if anything, help boost the Serbian government’s popularity at home.

The handling of NIS — Serbia’s oil giant, in which a pair of Russian state-owned companies control a majority stake — illustrates the more complicated reality of Washington’s approach. The Trump administration has granted sanctions waivers to NIS while Belgrade works to resolve the company’s Russian ownership structure. On August 28, Serbia secured another U.S. waiver, giving the company additional time as negotiations continue over the potential sale of the Russian stake. In sum, the Trump administration continues engaging with Belgrade even while pressing Serbia’s government on issues where interests clash.

The Trump-Vučić relationship, meanwhile, has so far fallen short of the close personal partnership that some observers anticipated after Trump’s 2024 electoral victory. For all the talk of an autocratic affinity between the two leaders based on shared resentment of “globalists,” there is limited evidence that such a relationship has emerged.

“Vučić has quite desperately attempted to meet with Trump, even traveling to Mar-a-Lago to do so, and has always been thwarted in his efforts,” noted Lily Lynch, editor-in-chief of the Balkanist Magazine. Lynch explained that Serbia’s government has “settled into a pragmatic, if somewhat distrustful, relationship with the [second] Trump administration.”

Whatever expectations existed in Belgrade in late 2024 and early 2025 that the second Trump administration would dramatically shift U.S. policy toward the Western Balkans to align much more closely with Serbia, Washington’s approach has so far appeared more transactional. The region remains relevant to the United States because of energy, regional stability, Russia, China, Kosovo, and European integration, but those interests compete with a much wider set of priorities.

Ultimately, the Trump administration is simultaneously pressuring Belgrade and seeking to continue cooperation. Nothing suggests that Washington is preparing to abandon its relationship with Serbia. Consecutive administrations, going back at least as far as the 2000s, have seen U.S. engagement with Serbia as necessary for stability in the Western Balkans. Belgrade’s arms transfers to Ukraine and Israel have also helped insulate Serbia’s government from criticism from officials in Washington over its refusal to implement European sanctions on Russia.

Balancing the Great Powers


Congressional pressure is also unlikely to produce a dramatic pivot in Serbian foreign policy. Belgrade has already been incrementally moving closer to the West while maintaining its broader strategy of balancing among competing powers.

This is particularly visible in Serbia-Russia relations. Belgrade has maintained ties with Moscow while cooperating with Western governments and supporting Ukraine in ways that complicate its traditional relationship with Russia. Yet these developments have not amounted to Serbia abandoning its broader balancing strategy.

“Vučić is basically allowed by the West to retain this already low level of relations with Russia, in return for support to Ukraine and cooperation with the West on some other issues. On the other hand, Russia is happy to see [itself wield] at least this much…influence [as it does] in Serbia,” Trapara said. “This way, Vučić attracts support by both [the West and Moscow] for stability of his regime.”

China, which has emerged as Belgrade’s most important non-Western economic and strategic partner, presents a different challenge. Beijing’s presence in Serbia is primarily economic, making the relationship structurally different from Serbia’s ties with Moscow. Miković warned that a worsening U.S.-China confrontation could eventually put Belgrade under greater pressure to distance itself from Beijing — a potentially much more difficult decision for Vučić, who traveled to China in May 2026 and hosted Chinese President Xi Jinping in May 2024.

Ultimately, Serbia has strong incentives to maintain relationships with the West, Russia, and China. Vučić has built considerable political capital around presenting himself as the leader capable of navigating between them.

Western pressure could strengthen Vučić at home


Besides Wilson and Keating, other Western policymakers seek to pressure Vučić’s government. Within the European Union, for which Serbia has been a formal candidate since March 2012, criticism has intensified over Serbia’s handling of the legacy of the 1990s Balkan wars. That issue has become particularly prominent following last month’s death of Ratko Mladić, the former Bosnian Serb military commander and convicted war criminal.

On September 3, a Serbian government plane flew Mladić’s body home to Serbia with his coffin wrapped in a Serbian flag. Days before Mladić’s funeral, held on September 7, EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos canceled a planned visit to Serbia, citing concerns about the glorification of Mladić, which Brussels warned “has no place in the EU or in EU candidate countries.” Just before the funeral, Sens. Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.), Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa), and Rep. Keith Self (R-Texas) called on authorities in Belgrade to “refrain from any association with the planned ceremonies and to ensure that no public statement or official act memorializes Mladic as anything other than what he was: a convicted architect of genocide.”

For some of Vučić’s domestic supporters, criticism from Washington or Brussels reinforces perceptions that Serbia faces unfair pressure from the West. Since Slobodan Milošević’s ouster in 2000, “the issue of Serbian support for war crimes indictees and convicted war criminals has been a constant irritant to U.S.-Serbia relations,” said Lynch. That dynamic could become particularly relevant as Serbia approaches its parliamentary elections.

Western pressure could ultimately help Vučić with his core electorate. “Most of his voters have a strong focus on national issues, and they are likely to interpret this pressure as proof that Vucic is doing ‘a good job of defending Serbia’s interests,’ which is why those ‘evil Westerners’ want to overthrow him,” observed Miković.

Trapara stressed how much is at stake for Serbia’s elections in terms of democratic health, the rule of law, independent institutions, a free press, and constitutionalism. At the same time, he argued that outside actors should be cautious about intervening in Serbia’s domestic affairs.

“A message to the foreigners, whether they launch strategic dialogues in support of the regime, or fruitlessly threaten sanctions to help the regime anyway, is that they should refrain from big Serbia-related political moves until we finish our job in the elections.”

item.title: How to prevent another disastrous war in the 'in-between' states
item.description:
Only a few days ago, Moldova’s ambassador to the U.S. said it was likely “not an accident” that a Russian jet-powered drone flew across his country’s territory while Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky’s plane was preparing to depart from Chișinău’s airport.

Armenia, meanwhile, continues to face Russian pressure over its increasing pro-Western orientation. And tensions continue to linger on Belarus’ western and southern borders following Ukrainian allegations this summer that the country is being used to advance Russia’s war effort.

Far from a disconnected smattering of events, these tensions stem from a larger regional crisis that predates — but was accelerated by — the Ukraine war. Bad U.S. policy played a crucial role in worsening this predicament.

In the decades following the end of the Cold War, the U.S. pursued a dual-track approach toward former Soviet states.

On the one hand, the West sought to integrate Russia — the strongest of all the new states and the USSR’s natural successor — as a junior partner into the U.S.-led liberal, capitalist world order. On the other, the U.S. and its European allies pursued a hedging policy across central and eastern Europe that included enlarging NATO up to Russia’s western borders, out of fear that Moscow’s historical autocratic and expansionist impulses would resurrect once more.

That dual policy “ultimately failed,” and the hedging “proved counterproductive,” as noted by Thomas Graham, one of America’s leading Russia scholars and practitioners. The Kremlin became convinced that America’s “true goal” was “eroding and containing Russian power,” a perception that drove Russia’s leaders to be “more determined to restore their might, push back against US initiatives in the former Soviet space, and drive wedges between NATO allies.”

Now that the post-Cold War unipolar era is definitively over, the U.S. must formulate a new policy toward the states stuck between NATO and Russia. This will be the key task — alongside preventing an escalation of the Ukraine war and rebalancing the trans-Atlantic relationship — for American policymakers focusing on Eurasia in the years ahead. The sum of these efforts will weigh upon two critical U.S. objectives: U.S. conventional retrenchment from Europe and the establishment of the conditions for long-term strategic stability between Russia and the West.

It was with these considerations in mind that we launched a Quincy Institute initiative focused on shaping U.S. policy toward Armenia, Azerbaijan, Belarus, Georgia, and Moldova — the so-called “in-between states.” In our newly-published inaugural report, we lay out a blueprint to help guide Washington’s policy toward this region in ways that will help advance America’s interests, support peace and prosperity, and avoid repeating the mistakes of the past.

A better approach to the in-between states would rely on a few key principles. One is that the U.S. has no vital interest at stake that necessitates it take on the risks of becoming a security guarantor for these countries. Another is that Washington should promote economic connectivity projects and political normalization efforts to strengthen Eurasian regional stability — and encourage in-between states to pursue multi-vector foreign policies that seek positive relations with all neighboring states.

Equally important here is the U.S. relationship with Russia. U.S. engagement in Eurasia must be accompanied by broader confidence-building measures with Russia, aimed at mitigating the risk of security spirals and misunderstandings.

This will require sustained dialogue with Moscow about what Washington is and is not doing, and the extent of its involvement in the in-between states. The Russians have demonstrated in both Georgia and Ukraine that they are willing to resort to the use of force to defend their interests in the in-between states, whereas NATO is not. The Kremlin has repeatedly made clear that it views the enlargement of the Western alliance into the in-between states as a red line.

It is, therefore, eminently sensible to take off the table the future expansion of NATO into former Soviet republics. Not only does it harm the foundations of Russia-West stability, but it also leads to greater instability for transatlantic partners and the in-between states themselves. When it comes to political and economic matters, however, the U.S. and the in-between states likely have greater room for maneuver.

In the context of the current security landscape, negotiating a compromise settlement to the Ukraine war will go a long way in assisting the U.S. with its other priorities across Eurasia and in the in-between states.

Washington’s greatest success to date in the in-between states is the August 8, 2025, announcement of the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP) at a White House ceremony with Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan, Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev, and President Donald Trump. Across Central Asia, the Caspian Basin, and the South Caucasus, American and European investments are increasing and political engagement is deepening. An important opportunity exists for TRIPP to become a key supply chain along the Middle Corridor, contributing to American efforts to strengthen U.S. access to the critical minerals essential to a modern economy and armed forces.

To ensure that this deepening engagement brings economic development and security to the South Caucasus, Washington must help Yerevan and Baku implement their peace agreement and facilitate normalization of Armenia-Turkey relations.

The Trump administration has achieved important successes through its engagement with Belarus, a country the U.S. had previously all but cast aside as an appendage to Russia. Pragmatic and consistent diplomatic work led to the release of several hundred political prisoners in exchange for sanctions relief. There remains much additional space for the development of political, diplomatic, and commercial ties between Washington and Minsk. A deliverable from a future potential meeting between Presidents Trump and Aleksandr Lukashenko may be full diplomatic normalization, which would open the door to increased trade and investment opportunities.

Final resolution of the remaining political-territorial disputes across the region — Transnistria in Moldova and Abkhazia and South Ossetia in Georgia — remains elusive. Nevertheless, a negotiated end to the Ukraine war alongside broader dialogue with Russia on European security matters would set the right conditions for progress in these other areas.

It’s high time for a new paradigm in the U.S. approach to the in-between states. Incorporating the strategic principles we lay out above into a new policy is vital to advancing American interests, fostering regional prosperity, and mitigating the risk of future crises in the Ukrainian mold.

item.title: How Trump's Iran operation turned into a forever war
item.description:
As the United States has struggled to secure its four primary objectives in the Iran War — achieving regime change, dismantling long-range ballistic missiles, eliminating nuclear enrichment, and halting Tehran’s support for regional proxies — U.S. officials have rolled out a series of tried-and-failed theories for how to achieve those goals.

In the past four weeks, Americans have watched their government attempt to inflict an economic victory against Iran through Operation Economic Outcast, tightening a sanctions regime which for decades has strangled Iran’s economy without resolving the underlying dispute.

Now, as that strategy flags, we have seen the Trump administration return to its older strategy of kinetic strikes against Iran. Those strikes, too, have failed to achieve their desired objectives.

Facing the prospect of a self-inflicted defeat, the U.S. has now proposed two new paths forward.

The first, reported by the Wall Street Journal last Wednesday, is an option to extend and formalize the current series of on-and-off strikes U.S. officials call this “mowing the lawn,” or a strategy of using periodic bouts of disproportionate force, as Israel did in Gaza prior to launching its full-scale, seemingly endless campaign after the Oct. 7 attacks of 2023. To support that option, the Pentagon has extended troop deployments in the Middle East through 2027.

The second option reportedly considered by the White House is for the U.S. to declare victory and walk away, with the Wall Street Journal reporting that Trump favors the idea. Among the supporters of the second option is Joe Kent, the former Director of the National Counterterrorism Center, who resigned in protest of the Iran War, and who has argued on X that the U.S. should “reset the terms of the deal” with Iran “by removing our troops & ships from the region.” The argument that the U.S should walk away and “declare victory” is growing increasingly popular even in establishment circles.

But given the historic limitations of sanctions to achieve political outcomes, coupled with Iran’s current demands, that strategy too appears unlikely to re-open the Strait of Hormuz and avert the economic consequences Iran’s leverage over the waterway will have on the global economy.

Political scientists have long doubted whether U.S. economic pressure and sanctions can shape political outcomes, particularly when the targeted state has little reason to believe these measures will be reversed in exchange for good behavior; researchers like David Siegel are quick to acknowledge that they “don’t work,” while U.S. officials like Janet Yellen have conceded the same point, noting that, while sanctions against Iran had caused a “real economic crisis,” they produced political outcomes “much less than we would ideally like.”

As Siegel — who most recently studied the failure of U.S. sanctions on Russia to redirect their state behavior toward U.S. and NATO interests — explains, “target states have strong incentives not to give in and sometimes even benefit from heightened levels of political support at home because they can now credibly blame their economic woes on a foreign imperial power.” Siegel argues that it's “probably more true today than ever before due to the fact that sanctioned states can turn to China.”

The low likelihood of economic pressure opening up the Strait of Hormuz is depressed even further by the fact that one of Iran’s preconditions for opening the Strait of Hormuz is the removal of sanctions, which would require a vote from Congress, where the proposal would face an uphill battle.

But perhaps the main reason walking away and declaring victory would fail to re-open the Strait and mitigate impending economic disaster is because Iran has tied freedom of navigation in the waterway to the U.S. reining in Israel, and the U.S. has long demonstrated it is unwilling to do so.

The June 17 agreement between the U.S. and Iran only required the U.S. force an Israeli withdrawal from Lebanon, and Washington failed to follow through. Now, subsequent provocations by the U.S. and Israel have led Iran to expand its ceasefire demands to other campaigns: in Iraq, in Yemen, and in Palestine.

Securing a deal to re-open the Strait and end the war is further complicated by the growing view around the world that the “Art of The Deal” author is simply incapable of making deals. Results of a 2025 Politico survey of diplomats from 15 countries show foreign officials describing Trump’s deal-making process as “reactive, with no clear direction,” while Trump has so far failed to resolve a proxy war in Ukraine that he promised to end “within 24 hours” of taking office. The White House has similarly failed to reach a peace deal in Gaza.

Under these conditions, the broader Iran War appears to be rapidly approaching what a chief executive of a Danish shipping firm described to the Financial Times as a “Ukraine-style stalemate.” Speaking to the outlet in August, the CEO of Torn explained how “the Gulf leadership has realised they need to prepare themselves for a prolonged situation that lasts not days or weeks but months or years,” adding that “with the U.S. acting the way it is, I think it is a dream world to imagine the world returns to the way it was 10 years ago in the foreseeable future.”

The consequences of that “prolonged situation” will soon be felt even more by American consumers, as Iran’s control over the Strait of Hormuz has pushed diesel prices to their highest ever levels. Averting economic catastrophe will therefore require the U.S. to meet conditions it has so far been unwilling to accept; merely declaring victory and walking away won’t do the trick.

item.title: The Houthis’ capture of Mocha has transformed the war in Yemen – and the geopolitics of the Red Sea
item.description:
The Houthis’ capture of Mocha has transformed the war in Yemen – and the geopolitics of the Red Sea Expert comment thilton.drupal 14 September 2026

Iran and its allies can now exert pressure on two strategic maritime chokepoints, with global implications. A more coherent international approach to Yemen is needed.

The Houthi armed group recently captured the strategic port city of Mocha in southwestern Yemen and advanced along the coast of the Bab al-Mandab Strait. This represents the most consequential change in territorial control in Yemen for years.

For Yemen, the offensive risks reopening a war that never formally ended but had become significantly less violent since the UN-mediated truce of 2022. For the wider region, the implications are also massive.

The Houthis’ new territorial position gives them much greater ability to influence maritime shipping through Bab al-Mandab, the narrow passage connecting the Gulf of Aden to the Red Sea and ultimately the Suez Canal. 

Together with Iran’s disruption of the Strait of Hormuz, Iran and its allies now have the capacity to exert pressure on two of the world’s most strategically important maritime chokepoints.

The Houthis have also launched attacks into Saudi Arabia, including against energy infrastructure, that have reportedly injured civilians. This also constitutes an escalation in the conflict and poses questions for Riyadh and its US ally. 

The fragmentation of Yemen’s anti-Houthi camp

Houthi forces, who control most of western Yemen, made a rapid push down the Red Sea coast last week. Government-aligned forces withdrew as the Houthis seized Mocha, surrounding areas and nearby islands. 

The Houthis benefited from surprise and military preparation. But the offensive also exposed the fragmentation of the anti-Houthi camp.

Government-aligned forces face coordination problems. The anti-Houthi forces include a variety of autonomous armed groups who were previously supported by different regional patrons and had competing political ambitions. Saudi attempts to bring them under a more coherent command structure since early 2026 have not erased years of fragmentation.

Meanwhile, the Houthis used the period of relative calm following the 2022 truce to recruit and mobilize personnel, improve domestic weapons production and expand their missile and drone capabilities. As a result, the Houthis now have more advanced capabilities than government forces in several areas. 

Bab al-Mandab, the Red Sea and the Horn of Africa 

The immediate international question is what the Houthis intend to do with their strengthened position around Bab al-Mandab.

The Houthis previously claimed they do not intend to impose formal transit fees on vessels passing through Bab al-Mandab. These assurances should be treated cautiously. There are indications that, since beginning their attacks on Red Sea shipping in 2023, the Houthis have been extracting informal payments from some shipping agencies in return for safe passage. 

The Houthis have also said that they are only attacking Saudi-linked ships in the Red Sea. However, a ship carrying Saudi oil may be owned, operated, financed, insured or chartered by companies in several different countries. It might also be delivering goods, or oil, to various countries. 

Houthi attacks on Saudi shipping therefore affect commercial interests far beyond Saudi Arabia, including in Europe and China.

Related work

The Houthi Red Sea blockade: Will collective maritime security be defended, or break down?

The Houthi advance also changes the security calculations of states with strategic interests in the Horn of Africa. 

Djibouti is just around 20 kilometres from Perim Island, which the Houthis now reportedly control. That places an armed movement with increasingly sophisticated drone, missile and maritime capabilities extremely close to a country that hosts US, Chinese, French, Italian and Japanese military bases. Other countries including Turkey and the United Arab Emirates also have significant security and commercial interests in the region. 

For now, the Houthis’ calculation is likely to be one of controlled escalation: converting military momentum into political and economic leverage without provoking an international response large enough to reverse their gains. But Yemen can no longer be treated as a distant theatre.

Trump faces difficult choice

Saudi Arabia has vowed to respond to Houthi attacks on its territory. Riyadh recently signed a mutual defence treaty with Turkey and Pakistan, but does not appear to have publicly called on either for assistance. 

The US, a close Saudi ally, reached a truce with the Houthis in May 2025, after conducting air strikes against the group following its attacks on shipping in the Red Sea. 

For US president Donald Trump, the recent Houthi advance creates a difficult dilemma. Trump has a close relationship with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, and the US retains a fundamental interest in Saudi security. At the same time, Washington has strong incentives to avoid reopening a direct war with the Houthis.

The existing truce gives both sides reasons for restraint. For Trump, preserving that arrangement helps keep the US away from another costly Middle Eastern military confrontation while it remains engaged in the Strait of Hormuz.

The Houthis have equally strong incentives to not be drawn into conflict with the US. The 2025 US air campaign against the Houthis caused serious damage. They have little interest in inviting a repeat.

This creates a peculiar situation: Washington and the Houthis both have reasons to avoid attacking one another, even while the Houthis increase pressure on one of the US’s closest regional partners.

That equilibrium, however, may not hold. If the Houthis escalate attacks on Saudi territory, especially if they attempt even limited ground incursions across the border, Washington could find itself pulled towards confrontation.

Yemenis pay the greatest cost 

Lost beneath the geopolitical consequences is the most predictable outcome of renewed war: Yemenis themselves will suffer most.

The country enters this phase of conflict with divided institutions, an economy devastated by more than a decade of war and declining international humanitarian support.

In Taiz alone, almost 50,000 people have reportedly been displaced since 3 September. In Mocha, the humanitarian consequences are particularly alarming. With health facilities collapsing or becoming inaccessible, local media reports indicate that more than 240 pregnant women in the region face the looming prospect of giving birth without access to functioning medical care.

Further disruption to ports, roads and supply chains will also drive up food, transport and fuel prices in a country heavily dependent on imports. 

While this new international dimension of Yemen’s war makes the country strategically more important to the world, it should not overshadow the plight of ordinary Yemenis. 

The need for a coherent international approach

Governments have tended to treat Saudi-Houthi negotiations, maritime security, humanitarian access to Yemen, Iran negotiations, the Yemeni government and wider Red Sea maritime security as separate issues. That approach is becoming increasingly difficult to sustain.

The Houthis are now able to influence global shipping, energy markets, Gulf security, the Horn of Africa and the calculations of major powers. A more coherent international approach is therefore needed.

For Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) states in particular, the latest escalation should be a warning. The GCC has not formulated a coherent policy on Yemen, influenced by disagreements between Gulf states and their different relationships with Yemeni factions. But the Houthis’ recent advances impact the entire GCC, so a Gulf-wide approach is needed. 

Recent developments should also challenge the idea that the Houthis can be contained through a collection of transactional arrangements. Bilateral maritime security deals may protect one country’s ships, while negotiations may temporarily calm one frontline. Military strikes can degrade individual capabilities.

But these approaches operate in silos. The Houthis do not. The movement simultaneously functions as a governing authority, an armed non-state actor, an Iranian regional ally and an increasingly important influence on maritime security.

The main policy challenge is therefore whether regional and international actors are prepared to develop a coherent approach to Yemen that connects the country’s political settlement with wider security issues in the Gulf, the Red Sea and the Horn of Africa. Ultimately, ignoring a crisis in Yemen does not contain it. It is only a matter of time before it becomes an international crisis.

We may soon face conflict with nation-states in a new model of warfare—one not defined by geography, but instead defined by AIs competing directly with one another. War has always been a ruthless teacher: adaptation, learning, and feedback determine who prevails. In the sixth domain of warfare—AI-driven conflict—that cycle of teaching accelerates beyond human limits. Machine systems do not just execute decisions; they absorb outcomes, update models, and refine strategy continuously and at scale. Strategy, planning, targeting, and execution collapse into a single, ongoing process of learning and acting at speeds no human command structure can match. Missiles, drones, satellites, and fleets remain, but only as instruments—physical endpoints through which AIs prosecute this competition. The real contest is not fought on terrain, but in cycles of learning and adaptation too fast for humans to comprehend. What matters is not force projection, but learning velocity; not command of terrain, but command of inference.

In this domain, doctrines like “human-in-the-loop” or even “human-on-the-loop” are not safeguards—they are handicaps. Any force that inserts human judgment into the learning cycle—whether tactical or strategic—will be systematically outpaced by one that does not. This is not a matter of doctrine or preference, but of competitive logic: systems that act and adapt faster gain an inherent advantage. If removing human constraints yields advantage, those constraints will vanish. This reality forces a stark choice: delegate authority to machines across the full stack of war and accept the risks of opacity and escalation, or retain human control and accept defeat at machine speed. The fog of war has not lifted—it has thickened into a machine-generated battlespace, a black-box system fighting and learning at a level humans can no longer fully observe or comprehend, let alone direct.

This transformation elevates intelligence from a supporting function to the central determinant of power. Models and compute provide capability, but intelligence—continuous, fused inputs from sensors across domains—provides the fuel that drives the system. The intelligence cycle itself describes the change: planning and direction, collection, processing and exploitation, analysis, production, and dissemination. In the sixth domain, machines run all of these functions. In an AI-versus-AI conflict, the side that sees more, sooner, and more clearly directs the learning loop itself. The advantage will not go simply to the best models, but to the systems that integrate intelligence fastest and most effectively. A slightly inferior model, continuously updated with superior, secure, low-latency data, will outperform a more advanced system operating on stale or fragmented inputs. Intelligence no longer informs decisions; it becomes inseparable from them.

The reflexive policy response in the West will be to constrain the leading AI companies in the name of control and safety. That instinct risks slowing the very learning cycles that determine advantage. Winning will require the opposite: accelerating innovation, tightly coupling it to national security objectives, and denying other nation-states key capabilities.

As in the nuclear era, this creates a parallel requirement for stability. The Great Powers share an interest—not in cooperation, but in using the technology to the benefit, rather than detriment, of society. To survive, we all need to understand each other’s AI capabilities and limits. Call it Mutually Assured AI Destruction: MAAID. Like its nuclear predecessor, deterrence will rest not on trust, but on verification, ambiguity, partial visibility, and intelligence where transparency fails. This is mutual self-interest under conditions of instability. In this domain, the equivalent of launch detection—recognizing decisive AI actions at inception—will be critical. Intelligence will need to continuously track, interpret, and outpace adversary AI systems, not only to compete, but to avoid surprise and uncontrolled escalation. What each side can see, and how quickly it can understand it, may determine whether competition remains bounded or spirals beyond control. An AI-era equivalent of the OPCW may therefore become necessary—an institution capable of inspecting, verifying, and monitoring advanced weapons AI systems under conditions of speed and opacity.

In the near future, humans will at best set initial conditions—policy, objectives, constraints—and then watch as their systems prosecute a war they can no longer meaningfully steer. Clausewitz wrote that war is the continuation of policy by other means. In the sixth domain, that distinction collapses. When systems translate intent into action, learn from the results, and adjust course continuously at machine speed, policy is no longer something periodically expressed through war. It is instantiated in code and executed as a continuous process. The side that learns fastest does not just win—it shapes the war itself.

Ukraine war spreads to Arctic as nuclear tensions escalate
item.description:
Last week, the war in Ukraine reached deep inside the Russian Arctic.

On September 9, Ukrainian drones struck two gas processing plants in the Yamalo-Nenets region, located about 1,900 miles from the Ukrainian border. This is Ukraine’s deepest strike on Russia since the war began. Arctic energy infrastructure in the Yamal region produces around 80% of Russia's natural gas.

Russian military analysts believe the Ukrainian drones were launched from Sumy, northern Ukraine, and reached all the way into Yamal with the help of Starlink. Ukraine’s Special Operations Forces announced, “Until today, this was considered an absolutely safe rear.”

The attack also shook European energy markets, as Europe buys large volumes of gas from the Yamal region. President Donald Trump later told Ukraine to stop attacking Russia’s diesel infrastructure, saying fuel shortages due to the strikes were “hurting the world,” without explicitly acknowledging the fact that the spike in global energy prices is largely driven by the Iran war.

This is the second time the Arctic has been drawn into the Ukraine war. Back in June 2025, Ukrainian drones, smuggled into Russia by truck, hit the Olenya air base on the Kola Peninsula, targeting Russia’s long-range strategic bombers that Moscow had considered safe because of their remote Arctic location.

No guardrails for deescalation


What makes these strikes especially dangerous is the lack of mechanisms to manage the next incident. Tensions between nuclear powers are already escalating in the Arctic. A confrontation in this region could quickly escalate into something much bigger.

Both the U.S. and Russia deploy strategic bombers and submarines north of the Arctic Circle. Russia uses the Arctic as a testing site for nuclear-powered cruise missiles and underwater drones.

Last week, anonymous Western officials told Reuters that, in April 2026, U.S., British, and Norwegian forces confronted Russian submersible vehicles that seemed to be practicing how to sabotage critical cables near Svalbard. The Russian Embassy in Oslo has dismissed the report as information warfare meant to justify NATO’s militarization of the Arctic.

Previously, the Arctic was the setting for confidence-building measures, force-posture information sharing, multilateral scientific cooperation, and programs that reduced the risks of miscalculation. Today, we are at dangerously low levels of trust, preventing such cooperative efforts. The region faces growing military activity and almost no mechanism to stop a stray drone or submarine maneuver from spiraling into an escalation neither side intends.

After the 2025 strike on Russia’s strategic bombers, George Beebe of the Quincy Institute noted with alarm that Western commentators celebrated the attack, largely ignoring the risks it posed to nuclear stability. An attack on the aviation leg of Russia's nuclear triad deserves far more sober reflection than the applause it received.

Arctic security dilemma


Against the background of the worsening conflict in Ukraine is a spiraling West-Russia confrontation. The current trajectory is a classic security dilemma: NATO builds up in the Arctic because of a perceived Russian threat, Russia builds up because of a perceived NATO threat, and round and round it goes. With every move, each side sees proof of the other’s hostility.

Following the accession of Finland and Sweden into NATO in 2023 and 2024, seven of the eight Arctic states (all but Russia) are members of the alliance. In February 2026, NATO launched Arctic Sentry, conjoining the alliance’s activities — including Denmark's Arctic Endurance and Norway's Cold Response — under a coherent operational framework coordinated through Joint Force Command in Norfolk, Virginia.

Arctic Sentry was announced a month after Trump raised tensions in the alliance with his threats to annex Greenland. NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte announced the mission as he lobbied Trump to drop the push to acquire the island.

European allies hoped that Arctic Sentry and talks with Washington would let NATO move on from the Greenland dispute and refocus on what they call Europe’s security priority: Russia and the war in Ukraine. Trump, meanwhile, continues to seek the acquisition of the Arctic island even as Europe invests $232 million to support Greenland.

Finland convened European leaders in Helsinki this week to discuss the “race with Russians and the Chinese for use and control of the Arctic.” The Finnish prime minister said “Europe has to be so strong that it won’t cross Russia’s mind to challenge us here in the north.”

Now, NATO exercises, such as Cold Response 26, are folded into the Arctic Sentry framework. This year’s exercise in Norway involved 30,000 troops from fourteen nations rehearsing a counterattack against an “enemy to the east.”

Russian officials have announced that Moscow will take measures to counter NATO in the Arctic. In parallel, Russia and China are increasing their Arctic security cooperation. In 2024, Russian and Chinese bombers conducted joint drills for the first time within Alaska's Air Defense Identification Zone, in international airspace.

That same year, the Chinese Coast Guard conducted its first-ever Arctic Ocean patrol alongside Russia’s Border Service. The U.S. responded by sending more troops and artillery to Alaska’s remote corners.

Restarting dialogue


To its credit, U.S. European Command (EUCOM) announced the restoration of military-to-military dialogue with Russia earlier this year. Norway also plans to discuss maritime security issues with Russia under the framework of the Agreement on the Prevention of Incidents at Sea (INCSEA).

With so much activity up north, it is reassuring to see some Arctic states gradually resume dialogue with Russia. Going forward, a circumpolar dialogue and channels for the other NATO member states that operate in the Arctic will be necessary.

The Ukraine war has impacted Russian-Chinese relations in the Arctic. From Russia’s point of view, turning to China has been a practical step in the face of diplomatic isolation, but it’s not necessarily Moscow’s first choice. Before 2022, Russia actively participated alongside its Western counterparts in maritime safety institutions like the Arctic Coast Guard Forum.

After the war started, the Western Arctic states condemned Russia’s military actions and suspended cooperation. Vladimir Kulishov, head of Russia's Border Service, explained that Moscow felt compelled to find new partners as a result. Russia invited China’s Coast Guard first as an observer to a Russian-led exercise, and later as a signatory to an official memorandum on maritime security cooperation.

The Western policy of isolating Russia has essentially left Moscow with little alternative but to pursue coordination with China. This has granted Beijing a strategic foothold in the Arctic — something the Pentagon regards as a top security threat. Previously, China had access to the Arctic mostly through Russia’s tolerance rather than its partnership.

The recent escalations are a warning that the guardrails and old rules are gone. If we want to prevent the region from turning into a permanent battlefield, all Arctic states need to get serious about risk reduction.

The Ukraine war severed decades of productive Arctic cooperation. As the search for peace in Ukraine now resumes, all Arctic states should enhance diplomatic channels, especially military-to-military dialogue like the channels that EUCOM and the Norwegian armed forces are pursuing with Russia. Multilateral cooperation between Arctic states’ coast guards is also crucial.

The new status quo — a state of ever-increasing tensions between nuclear-armed powers — is simply too risky to bear.

We Are In An Unpredictable War Of Attrition
item.description:
We are squarely in the target sights of ‘Unintended Consequences.’

What do I mean by this? Think of it as a broad spectrum of possible consequences when missiles and drones are being slung back and forth between Iran and U.S. Navy vessels and bases, and the energy and commercial facilities and ships of its Gulf allies. On one end of the spectrum, accidents happen: think the inadvertent U.S. airstrike on the girls’ school at the beginning of the war, and the more recent ‘wedding party’ casualties when a U.S. missile struck a nearby communications tower. These are tragedies for all involved. On the other side, an Iranian missile made its way through U.S. air defenses to strike a U.S. military facility in Jordan, resulting in the deaths of three U.S. troops. The latter resulted in a robust U.S. military response that targeted a variety of Iranian military facilities. This was a success for Iran and a tragedy for America.

On the other end of the spectrum, what if one of Iran’s ballistic missiles successfully navigates to its target - a U.S. base or navy vessel, for example - and significant U.S. casualties, dead and/or wounded, result? The U.S. administration is likely to come under tremendous political pressure to respond with overwhelming force. This could elevate the stakes even higher, cutting off any chance of a negotiated settlement, remote as it currently is. And with the regime already having been severely degraded militarily, and its leadership ranks diminished, what does that leave in terms of targets? More of the same?

It could also result in calls to withdraw U.S. forces, given the antipathy of a majority of the U.S. population to a war they view as unnecessary, ill-advised, and ill-managed. This would leave Iran in a weakened yet still dangerous posture, with the ability to pressure the world economy at will going forward. Neither option is appealing.

Oh, and by the way, notwithstanding the administration’s verbal gymnastics, this is very much a war.

D-Day Sanctions Regime

On the surface, this appears to be a pretty solid strategy, or at least better than what has been tried to date: Simply squeeze the Iranian economy until the regime cries uncle. It is already having an impact and will likely continue to compound the pain. But it is neither simple nor clear-cut. Who will it actually impact, how badly, and when? A total blockade means not just money or arms. It means no food. It means no medicine. And a host of other basic necessitates. The Iranian people will feel it first, particularly the young, the old, and the sick. Regime insiders, including the leadership and their loyal (for now) security forces, will be the last to see the effects.

And we have already seen Russia and China reject complying with the secondary sanctions that comprise the heart of this enhanced effort. So, no one knows what will happen if they choose to challenge the blockade; It is highly unlikely that U.S. forces will use force against Chinese vessels attempting to access Iranian ports. And that does not take into account less overt (read clandestine) interactions - intelligence sharing, weapons system development, sabotage efforts against Gulf country facilities, including pipelines, etc. - that would further evade and/or erode the U.S. advantage.

So, while there will be pain, and lots of it, as I said in a recent BBC interview, there remain many unknowns. Informal smuggling networks have abounded in the region for Millenia. The regime will utilize every trick they have learned since the ‘79 revolution while building a ‘resistance economy’ to get around the blockade/sanctions. And potentially with the implicit, if not explicit, support of two major world powers. In the end, this does not presage the near-term submission of a regime that values survival above all else. This remains very much a test of wills.

Furthermore, what happens when the world sees the Iranian people starving before their eyes? I’m not sure they will countenance this for long.

So, Who Has More at Stake?

The U.S. people are seeing higher gas prices at the pump, rising food costs, overall inflation, and more. This is painful, but certainly not existential, at least not yet. The increasingly negative impact on the world economy stands to worsen things considerably if the status quo continues for too long, so Americans are watching closely. And the mid-terms are fast approaching.

The Iranian people are seeing the destruction of their economy, their country, and potentially their very way of life. It is very much existential. The specter of a thundering locomotive of new sanctions bearing down on them must certainly be terrifying. I have no doubt many Iranians blame the Islamic regime for bringing this down upon them. But as things worsen, they may turn against the U.S. and its allies for abandoning them to the depredations of the regime.

The Iranian regime most certainly views this as an existential threat, notwithstanding its rhetoric. They would be fools not to. But Netanyahu’s 2 September statement that the Israeli government is, “working to bring down this regime and defeat it,” accompanied by Trump’s 2 September statement publicly questioning, “when the Iranian people would rise up and fight,” is unlikely to motivate them to negotiate. They will need to be forced to submit. My experience with Iranians tells me that the harder you press, the more resistant they become. Uncharted territory indeed. We will see.

China and Russia both have an adversarial relationship with the U.S. and important interests vis-à-vis Iran: military for Russia (drones) and commercial for China (oil). Why would either go out of their way to assist the United States in removing itself from a self-imposed disaster that is distracting it from issues they care about while diminishing its military capabilities, all with minimal effort? That is a question that remains to be answered.

Speaking of Regime Change

U.S. political leadership answers to the American people at the ballot box. The system is a bit creaky at the moment, but (for now) it remains intact.

The Islamic regime, by design, does not answer to the Iranian people. Iran’s elections are truly rigged, primarily by the Guardian Council’s ability to reject candidates for office, but also with an increasing willingness to falsify election results. And in the end, the Supreme Leader is able to reject any initiative or law he disagrees with. We have seen the results when the Iranian people see no recourse for accountability by the regime: people in the streets, followed by blood in the streets.

Without substantial outside support, of which we have so far seen little evidence, the populace will be hesitant to go back to the streets, knowing that if they do, they are on their own. It could happen if things get bad enough, and it is possible it might even ultimately be successful, but it is almost certain to be a massacre, followed by chaos and a very uncertain end. Yet another example of unintended consequences.

Where Are We Now?

For the moment - and this may already have changed as I write this - we are back in what I refer to as a Hyperbolating phase, where we are seeing threats/counterthreats being tossed back and forth with abandon. Most of these statements are utterly meaningless and can be ignored. It appears both sides are waiting to see who blinks first.

U.S. messaging appears to be somewhat disjointed, contradictory, and lacking an overall strategy, with the President, the only real decision-maker, continually wandering on and off the path of others in his administration: Trump - I don’t care/where are the Iranians?; Hegseth - continued confrontation; Bessent - economic asphyxiation; Rubio - no nuclear weapon/economic pressure; Vance - not a war/intermittent containment. You could claim this is purposeful to keep Iran uncertain and off balance, but it should not be doing the same to Americans. President Trump failed to bring the American people on board beforehand with a coherent (and honest) case for war and an actual strategy for winning it. The continued shuffling of various justifications we have seen from the administration serves simply to stir the mix of confusion.

I get the distinct feeling that, given the fast approaching mid-terms and the deep hole they have dug for themselves, the administration just hopes that something/anything works so they can walk away from what is clearly a foreign policy disaster.

Iran messaging, on the other hand, appears, at least to me, to be a bit more coordinated if not strategic. While most Iranian government leaders are defiantly threatening massive retaliation for continued U.S. strikes (hyperbole), including the military (both Artesh - regular military and IRGC - Revolutionary Guards), the Parliament and its Speaker Ghalibaf (“U.S. actions will not go unanswered”), and the Foreign Affairs Ministry (claiming “war crimes” by the U.S.), the lone man on an island is the Iranian President, Pezeshkian; “we do not seek war but will respond,” and, “Iran remains open to negotiations, under the June MOU”. It is important to realize that the Iranian President has virtually no policymaking role in Foreign affairs, so his statements should be given less weight than others. But he would never make this offer without the approval of the IRGC, the Supreme National Security Council and, most likely, the Supreme Leader (or whoever is speaking for him). As I have written previously, I believe that the vagueness of the original June MOU was oddly advantageous to Iran and served to lead us directly back to where we currently are. So… this would seem to indicate negotiations are at least still on the table, just not under conditions particularly favorable to the U.S.

Where Are We Going?

Military escalation? A slow grinding pressure on the regime, testing their willingness to allow their people to suffer? Or a return to the negotiating table?

Who knows? There is no simple or painless way out of this.

Unintended consequences, after all.
